articles.title: Bradford skin cancer waiting times cut by new AI technology
articles.summary: Clinic can now see more patients and get results faster thanks to new scanning technology.
articles.body:
Staff at an NHS clinic using artificial intelligence (AI) to detect skin cancer sooner have said the technology could be a "game changer".

The dermatology team at St Luke's Hospital in Bradford adopted the new system in April to examine suspicious skin lesions.

The quick scanning means that 32 patients can be seen in each session, compared to 24 before AI was introduced.

Consultant plastic surgeon Mr Zakir Shariff said the technology has had a "big impact" on waiting times and the number of unnecessary procedures.

The AI system is called DERM, which stands for Deep Ensemble for the Recognition of Malignancy.

The company behind the technology, Skin Analytics, claims the AI is 99.9% accurate at ruling out melanoma cases.

A healthcare assistant takes three photographs of the suspicious mole or lesion and then uploads them to the system, which analyses them in minutes.

Patients with benign cases are offered advice and discharged, while those identified as suspicious are referred to a specialist as part of a one-stop clinic.

In Bradford, every image is double-checked by a clinician to make sure the diagnosis is correct.

"This has had a big impact on all the bottlenecks – right from waiting times for patients to unnecessary investigations being done and to being seen by a clinician," Shariff said.

"It's amazing, I mean it's excellent, at giving non-cancerous diagnosis quite quickly, within minutes.

"It's had an impact for patients and for the department," he said.

The number of unnecessary biopsies has dropped by about 10% since the AI was introduced, according to the trust.

Laurence Patten was urgently referred to the clinic by his GP because of a suspicious mole on his back.

The 73-year-old has multiple myeloma and a previous history of skin cancer on his right forearm, known as squamous cell carcinoma.

Images of his mole were flagged as suspicious by the AI but a subsequent examination by a specialist doctor suggested it was likely benign.

The mole will be removed and tested to confirm the diagnosis.

Patten, a former builder, said he was pleased to have been seen so promptly.

"It's not ticking away in my mind, which is one of the biggest things with cancer.

"The sooner they find things, the quicker they can sort it," he said.

Dr Nader Ghaderi, an associate specialist in dermatology, who examined Patten, said the AI was right to flag his case.

"If he was not checked by AI and was checked by a doctor, the doctor would have done a biopsy or definitely a follow-up would have been arranged; although the findings are pointing towards a benign lesion," he said.

The AI technology has been recommended by the National Institute for Clinical Excellence (NICE) for use in the NHS for the next three years, while evidence is collected.

It is now deployed in 40 NHS hospital trusts and Bradford Teaching Hospitals was the first in Yorkshire to adopt it.

Tom White, the trust's general manager who oversees dermatology, said early evidence suggested the use of AI could be a "game changer".

"It will significantly reduce the number of urgent referrals that require review by dermatologists, reducing waiting times and allowing us to concentrate on the most urgent cases," he said.

There are around 5,000 referrals every year for suspected skin cancer in Bradford, according to the Trust.

However, only about 8%, or 400 patients, are found to have malignant cancer.

articles.title: Nobel Prize for Medicine for showing inner workings of the brain
articles.summary: US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and his German colleagues Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel have been awarded for their work.
articles.body:
US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and his German colleagues Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel have been awarded this year's Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their work in the field of optogenetics.

Their research has helped scientists learn more about the inner workings of the brain, to better understand how the human mind works.

The Nobel Committee praised the trio for laying the foundation of a new era in neuroscience by revealing how to switch on and off neural circuits behind "specific memories, feelings, and behaviours relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders".

In clinical medicine, researchers are using the method to try to restore sight in people with visual impairment .

"Optogenetics has fundamentally altered our understanding of the brain," the Nobel Assembly said.

"Every day brings new discoveries, helping to solve one of humanity's great mysteries: how our incredible brain works."

The winners said it was "absolutely wonderful" to get the award, and that it was an honour to share the accolade with friends.

The three men will also share the £900,000 (12 million Swedish kronor) prize money.

Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine, explained: "Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of."

Before, the inner workings behind feelings, behaviours and bodily functions were more of a mystery to scientists.

Optogentics is a way to illuminate brain pathways, using a special protein borrowed from algae that scientists use to control cell electrical activity using light.

In the early 2000s, Hegemann and Nagel discovered channelrhodopsin, the algal protein with unique properties.

Deisseroth worked out how to use this light controlled protein to switch on nerve cells in the brains of mice.

Researchers have since been able to study nerve cells and pathways in animals to see and discover more about what they do.

The Nobel Committee said: "Using light, researchers are now able to switch individual neural circuits on or off in the brain. They can bring memories to life, create feelings, drive behaviours and study the types of neurons that are involved in various psychiatric and neurological disorders."

That is providing important insights into how the nervous system interacts with various cells in other areas of the body, such as in the heart and gut, the committee added.

Researchers have also taken "the first steps" towards using optogenetics as a medical treatment, the committee explained.

In ongoing clinical trials, scientists have been working to restore vision in people who have become blind due to retinitis pigmentosa, a disease that destroys the eye's rods and cones.

By inserting a special protein in the damaged region of the eye, the patient regained some vision when wearing special glasses emitting light. This switched on the therapeutic algae proteins.

articles.title: 7 everyday mistakes could be quietly damaging your vision, eye doctor warns
articles.summary: An NYU ophthalmologist reveals how sun exposure, eye rubbing, dehydration and poor sleep may silently accelerate aging in the eyes and impact vision.
articles.body: As Americans live longer, experts say everyday habits may be taking a toll on eye health earlier than expected. Dr. Douglas Lazzaro, professor of ophthalmology at NYU Langone Health, warned that several everyday habits may be silently affecting eye health. Age-related eye conditions include glaucoma, which damages the optic nerve, and cataracts, a clouding of the eye’s lens that can block light and blur vision. POPULAR ERECTILE DYSFUNCTION DRUG LINKED TO EYE DISEASE THAT CAN CAUSE IRREVERSIBLE VISION LOSS While genetics and aging remain major drivers of many eye diseases, avoiding the following common mistakes may help slow their progression and protect vision, Lazzaro told Fox News Digital. No. 1: Not protecting eyes from the sun While exposure to sunlight is beneficial for overall metabolic health and longevity, failing to protect the eyes from the sun may lead to accelerated damage. Lazzaro pointed to research suggesting that long-term ultraviolet exposure may contribute to macular degeneration and the progression of cataracts. POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS FACE NUMEROUS LAWSUITS OVER RARE 'EYE STROKE' LINKED TO VISION LOSS In the doctor's own practice, cataracts are appearing five to 10 years earlier than they did three decades ago, which he believes may be linked to ultraviolet light exposure. He recommends wearing sunglasses in bright, sunny conditions to help protect the eyes, including the lens and retina. No. 2: Reading in poor light Reading in poor lighting can increase eye strain and make it harder to focus, particularly with age, according to Lazzaro. "As we get older, our eyes have more difficulty seeing under certain lighting conditions," he told Fox News Digital, noting that older adults may have more difficulty adjusting to darker environments. "If you're going be reading, and it's not a bright, sunny day outside, or you're not inside with bright lights, you should increase the lighting," he recommended. No. 3: Not eating a healthy diet Research suggests that a nutritious diet may protect eye health by reducing the risk of diabetes and cardiovascular disease, both of which can affect vision. "Diet is important," Lazzaro said. "There's certainly a lot of known data about poor diets [contributing] to poor cardiovascular health, and that same thing can apply with the eye." DIET CHANGE TIED TO ‘YOUNGER’ BIOLOGICAL AGE IN OLDER ADULTS AFTER 4 WEEKS High cholesterol and high blood pressure can worsen diabetic eye disease, even when patients may not realize those conditions are affecting their vision, according to the doctor. Researchers are also exploring whether gut health may influence retinal health, although that connection is still emerging. No. 4: Not staying hydrated Another condition that becomes increasingly common with age is dry eye, in which a lack of tear production and oil secretion causes red, itchy, irritated eyes. This condition can be exacerbated by lifestyle factors like dehydration, Lazzaro noted. Staying hydrated helps keep the cornea properly moisturized, he said. "We always tell our patients, particularly in the summer, if they're going out on a hot day … make sure to hydrate, because not only will it dry out the body … but it can dry out your corneas." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ No. 5: Getting poor sleep Getting adequate sleep helps support overall health, and there’s "good evidence" that patients who don’t sleep well, particularly those with sleep apnea, may experience increased eye pressure, according to Lazzaro. People with sleep apnea also appear to face higher rates of glaucoma and certain vascular eye conditions, similar to their increased cardiovascular risk, the doctor said. "They also have an increased incidence of vascular phenomena in the eye … People who don't sleep well have fluctuations in their circulation at night." No. 6: Rubbing the eyes Eye rubbing is considered a risk factor for keratoconus, a progressive eye disease where the cornea begins to dome and bulge out in a cone shape, although experts' opinions differ on whether it can directly cause the disease, according to Lazzaro. Patients with keratoconus often rub their eyes frequently, he noted, and repeated rubbing can potentially change the shape of the cornea — one reason he "strongly" advises against the habit. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER No. 7: Delaying routine eye doctor visits Because glaucoma often develops without symptoms, a comprehensive eye exam is frequently the only way to detect it early, Lazzaro said. Glaucoma is known as a "silent disease" that can lead to blindness, the doctor noted. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "Its nickname is 'the silent thief of sight,'" he said. "Sometimes the only way you know you have glaucoma is by going to the ophthalmologist. It’s a disease that we see with increasing frequency as we get older." Lazzaro recommends that adults get annual eye exams, rather than waiting until age-related vision changes begin. Presbyopia — the gradual loss of the ability to focus on nearby objects — commonly develops in middle age and often leads to the need for reading glasses. "The only way you know you have glaucoma is by going to the ophthalmologist." "Patients will come in at some point, usually between 40 and 50, and say they can't see up-close anymore; it happened overnight," he said. Sun exposure may contribute not only to cataracts and macular degeneration, but also to cancers of the eyelid, Lazzaro said. "Most of them can be removed locally without a big problem if diagnosed early," he added.

articles.title: Here’s Exactly How Often to Eat Fish to Support Brain Health, According to a Dietitian
articles.summary: Fish and seafood are packed with nutrients like protein, antioxidants and brain health-boosting fats. Here’s often to eat these foods, according to a dietitian.
articles.body: Fish and seafood are packed with nutrients like protein, antioxidants and brain-boosting healthy fats. But many Americans don’t eat enough fish to get the full benefits from these foods. Even if you don’t consider yourself a big fish fan, it’s worth exploring the vast amount of healthy seafood choices out there because of the unique benefits the foods provide for your long-term health. Nutrition Tip of the Day: Eat Fish Twice a Week to Boost Brain Health “Eating fatty fish, like salmon, sardines or tuna, twice a week supports brain health,” says Natalie Rizzo, registered dietitian and TODAY nutrition editor. These types of fish provide the specific types of healthy fat that are linked to better brain health. Why It Matters There are three main categories of healthy omega-3 fatty acids, as TODAY.com explained previously. That includes alpha-linolenic acid (ALA), eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA). “While foods like walnuts, chia seeds and flaxseeds provide ALA, our bodies convert only a small amount of ALA into EPA and DHA,” Rizzo says. “Therefore, the main source of EPA and DHA is fatty fish.” In one study of healthy adults, people who ate fish at least twice a week had healthier-looking white matter, which acts as the brain’s communication network, than people who ate fish less often, Rizzo explains. And other research links DHA deficiency with cognitive decline, she adds. How to Get Started If you’re not used to cooking fish at home, it can be a little daunting. And some types of seafood have a stronger “fishy” taste than others, which may or may not be a selling point for you. Dietitians previously recommended sardines and salmon as two of the healthiest types of fish to eat. They’re both packed with brain-boosting DHA, but are also both on the more intense end of the fish flavor spectrum. For a milder alternative to salmon, registered dietitian Samantha Cassetty previously recommended looking to arctic char and trout. Try these recipes: Grilled Trout with Asparagus and Sorrel SauceBrown-Bag Arctic Char with Potatoes, Olives and HerbsSunny Anderson’s Barbecue Salmon And, for a similarly convenient tinned fish alternative to sardines, a classic canned tuna will get the job done. Try making your tuna salad with some plain Greek yogurt to pack even more protein into the meal. TODAY’s Expert Tip of the Day series is all about simple strategies to make life a little easier. articles.summary: Savannah Guthrie mourned the death of social media influencer Brooke Eby, revealing Oct. 5 on TODAY that she died from ALS on Oct. 1 at the age of 37.
articles.body: Savannah Guthrie mourned the death of social media influencer Brooke Eby, revealing Oct. 5 on TODAY that she died from ALS on Oct. 1 at the age of 37. Savannah announced the news while recalling Eby’s “remarkable battle” against the disease. “(It was) remarkable for the way she bore that devastating diagnosis, which she received at the age of 33, with courage, openness and humor,” Savannah said. “She was determined to share every aspect of her journey, the videos she posted on social media often hilarious, garnering her a devoted online following of millions.” Savannah continued by marveling at how Eby always had a smile in the face of her condition. “Even as her body began to fail her, she kept up her fight, and kept posting, with her trademark humor and spirit,” she said, while noting she created ALStogether, a community for people with ALS. Eby drew legions of followers on TikTok by chronicling her experience with ALS, posting videos while sharing what life is like with the disease, adding a lighthearted touch to her fatal medical diagnosis. Savannah initially spoke with Eby on TODAY in 2023 when she explained how she remained so cheerful, despite her condition. “Brooke, you are the most cheerful person I can imagine who has such a serious diagnosis,” Savannah said. “What gives you that joie de vivre, this joy?” “Levity is my superpower,” she said. “And it’s really how I’m bringing my story to the world. I’m trying to use humor and really let ALS be heard.” She also was determined to use her social media videos and her own story to raise awareness of ALS. “I think people are so scared to talk about a terminal diagnosis and death and what that looks like in a young person, but if you see yourself in me and you’re able to laugh with me, then hopefully people are taking away more about ALS,” she said. It’s a sentiment she shared in an essay she wrote for TODAY.com in 2023. “ALS is very much still a hopeless disease,” she wrote. “The scary part is that so much is unknown about why people are affected by it, but if any of my videos can help start conversations to drive awareness — and then drive pressure and resources — then maybe we can find a cure, or a way to make this a livable disease.”

articles.title: Nobel medicine prize honours US and German scientists for optogenetics work
articles.summary: The winners of the Nobel Prizes in physics, chemistry, literature, peace and ‌economics will be announced in the week.
articles.body:
American scientist Karl Deisseroth and Germans Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel have won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their pioneering discoveries on light and optogenetics that have helped understand ⁠how the brain works.

The Nobel Assembly of Sweden’s Karolinska Institute medical university said on Monday that Deisseroth, 54, Hegemann, 71, and Nagel, 73, were honoured “for their discovery of a molecular switch for nerve cells”.

Optogenetics involves controlling nerve signals with light, and helps researchers understand how specific cell types contribute to behaviours like learning, fear, addiction and movement.

“Optogenetics has fundamentally altered our understanding of the brain. Every day brings new discoveries, helping to solve one of humanity’s great mysteries: how our incredible brain works,” the Nobel Assembly said.

Thomas Perlmann, the secretary-general of the ⁠Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institute, added that optogenetics “makes it possible to switch on, or off, the activity of individual nerve cells in a living brain”.

“This method is now being used in laboratories around the world to reveal the brain’s mysteries,” Perlmann added.

“Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel committee, said in a statement.

Researchers also hope optogenetics could improve cochlear implants, allowing more precise stimulation of the auditory nerve than current electrical devices.

Deisseroth, 54, is a professor at Stanford University in the US, while Hegemann, 71, is a neuroscience professor at Humboldt University of Berlin. Nagel, 73, is a biophysics professor at the University of Wurzburg. The three of them will share a prize sum amounting to 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2m).

“All three said the same thing: that they ⁠thought it was absolutely wonderful to receive the prize with the other two who they call their friends – that it’s such an honour to receive the prize together,” Perlmann said.

Nobel laureates are chosen by expert committees appointed by the prize-awarding institutions. The physiology or medicine prize traditionally opens the annual Nobel announcements, with the Nobel Prize for physics announced on Tuesday, followed by the chemistry prize on Wednesday and the literature prize on Thursday.

But perhaps the most keenly anticipated award is that due on Friday, the peace prize – the only Nobel to be awarded in Oslo. Experts have suggested the jury could choose a laureate this year who enjoys broad consensus, after last year’s controversial winner , Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado.

Laureates receive their awards on December 10, the anniversary of Nobel’s death, in ceremonies attended by Sweden’s and Norway’s royal families, with banquets held in their honour.

articles.title: Everyone Is Talking About Ferritin Levels. How Much Does It Really Matter for Your Health?
articles.summary: A hemotologist explains what ferritin is and how it can impact your iron levels. Learn how to check your ferritin and how your doctor might interpret your results.
articles.body: Ferritin is having a moment. The iron-storage protein is showing up more and more in conversations about fatigue, wellness and blood work, but what does your ferritin number actually tell you? Ferritin is a blood marker that gives doctors a window into how much iron is stored in the body. With recent changes to the guidelines for diagnosing iron deficiency, ferritin levels are getting even more attention. Earlier this month, the American Society of Hematology (ASH) released new guidelines for diagnosing iron deficiency, recommending higher ferritin thresholds than have traditionally been used. The goal is to identify iron deficiency earlier, before it develops into iron deficiency anemia. So, what does your ferritin number actually tell you? Here’s what to know. What Is Ferritin? “Ferritin is a protein that stores iron in our bodies and is a reflection of how much iron storage we have,” says Dr. Angela Weyand, a clinical professor of pediatric hematology-oncology at the University of Michigan Medical School and a member of the expert panel that established the new ASH guidelines. Think of ferritin as your body’s iron savings account. The body stores iron so it can access it when needed. Iron is essential for making hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout the body. But iron also plays roles in muscle metabolism, cellular function and other processes. Why Is Ferritin Important? Iron has many functions, but the most important is making red blood cells. When your body doesn’t have enough iron coming in or is losing more iron than it can replace, it starts drawing from iron stores. As those stores become depleted, ferritin levels fall. That’s why ferritin is an important tool for identifying iron deficiency. “The best test for most people to assess iron deficiency is ferritin,” Dr. Weyand says. Iron deficiency is extremely common. A 2025 review in JAMA estimated that iron deficiency affects about 2 billion people worldwide and about 14% of adults in the United States. When iron stores are depleted, the body may not have enough iron available for processes involved in energy production, muscle function and cognitive function. Some people have no obvious symptoms of iron deficiency, while others may experience fatigue, weakness, dizziness, headaches, shortness of breath, difficulty concentrating or restless leg syndrome. As iron deficiency becomes more severe and progresses to iron deficiency anemia, symptoms can become more pronounced, including fatigue, weakness, difficulty concentrating and reduced exercise or work capacity. The important distinction is that iron deficiency and iron deficiency anemia are not the same thing. Iron deficiency can occur before anemia develops, which is one reason ferritin is useful — it can help identify depleted iron stores before the deficiency progresses further. Who Is at Risk for Iron Deficiency? Iron deficiency can happen to anyone, but some people are at higher risk, including those who: Have heavy menstrual bleedingAre pregnantHave recently experienced significant blood lossHave certain gastrointestinal conditions that affect iron absorptionHave chronic inflammatory conditionsHave increased iron needs, such as during periods of growth Diet can also play a role in iron stores. Plant foods including beans, lentils, tofu, nuts, seeds and fortified cereals, contain non-heme iron, which isn’t absorbed as well as the heme iron found in meat and seafood. As a result, vegetarians and vegans should eat almost twice the amount of daily iron, as compared to those who eat meat. While diet can be one contributor to low ferritin levels, blood loss and problems with iron absorption are also common causes of iron deficiency. If a blood test shows that your ferritin is low, your health care provider can help determine what may be causing the iron deficiency and whether treatment is needed. What Are the New Ferritin Recommendations? For years, laboratories have typically determined a “normal” ferritin range by looking at the distribution of ferritin levels in a population. But ASH says these statistical reference ranges aren’t necessarily the best way to determine when iron stores are too low. A laboratory reference range describes what is statistically typical in a particular population. But being outside that range doesn’t necessarily mean a person has a medical condition, and being inside it doesn’t always mean there is no clinically meaningful issue. “The recommendations changed because using reference ranges, which take a presumed healthy population and define ‘normal’ using a standard curve doesn’t work for a condition that affects so many people,” Dr. Weyand says. “The new recommendations are based on clinical outcomes and measures, rather than relying on a statistical analysis.” She says these types of clinical outcomes are also used for other conditions that affect a large population, such as high cholesterol. That means some people who previously received a “normal” ferritin result may now meet the criteria for iron deficiency. The new guidelines recommend these ferritin thresholds for diagnosing iron deficiency: Children ages 9 months to 4 years: 20 ng/mL or lowerAdults: 30 ng/mL or lowerCertain high-risk groups, including people with heavy menstrual bleeding and pregnant individuals with anemia: 50 ng/mL or lower How Do You Check Your Ferritin Levels? Ferritin is measured through a simple blood test. If you’re experiencing symptoms that could be related to iron deficiency, have a risk factor, such as heavy menstrual bleeding or pregnancy, or have had iron deficiency in the past, ask your healthcare provider whether checking your ferritin makes sense. And don’t be surprised if your ferritin result doesn’t come back with a simple “normal” or “abnormal” answer. There are many factors to take into consideration when assessing ferritin status, but the new ASH recommendations are intended to help clinicians recognize iron deficiency more consistently. Should You Take Iron If Your Ferritin Is Low? If your ferritin is low, the next step is figuring out why. Treatment may involve increasing dietary iron, taking an iron supplement or addressing an underlying cause, such as blood loss or an absorption problem. But don’t start taking high-dose iron simply because your ferritin is on the low end of normal. Too much iron can be harmful, and the appropriate treatment depends on whether you actually have iron deficiency, what’s causing it and your overall health. If you’re concerned about your ferritin level, talk with your healthcare provider about how to interpret the result alongside your symptoms, medical history and other iron studies. What Does High Ferritin Mean? While low ferritin can be a sign of iron deficiency, a high ferritin level doesn’t necessarily mean you have too much iron. Ferritin can increase in response to inflammation, so elevated levels can occur with acute or chronic inflammation, chronic alcohol consumption, liver disease, renal failure and metabolic syndrome. High ferritin can also have other causes, including iron overload, certain cancers or repeated blood transfusions. That’s why an elevated ferritin result needs to be interpreted in context with your health care provider. In other words, a high ferritin number isn’t automatically a sign that you have too much iron, just as a “normal” ferritin number doesn’t always rule out iron deficiency.

articles.title: Alzheimer’s risk linked to compound found in popular joint health supplements
articles.summary: University of Florida researchers found glucosamine users with mild cognitive impairment were 25% more likely to progress to dementia in a new study.
articles.body: Many older adults turn to glucosamine to manage aging joints, but for individuals with mild cognitive impairment, the supplement could be linked to faster progression to Alzheimer’s disease. To investigate how glucosamine affects dementia risk and mortality, University of Florida researchers analyzed medical records of patients with mild cognitive impairment, tracked laboratory mouse models and examined healthy versus Alzheimer’s-affected human brains. The study, which was published in Nature Metabolism, focused on glycosylation, a natural process where brain cells attach small chains of sugar to proteins. 7 NEW DEMENTIA RISK FACTORS REVEALED — INCLUDING ONE MILLIONS STRUGGLE WITH "You can think of these sugar chains as the labels and fittings on a machine part — they help a protein fold correctly, get shipped to the right place in the cell and connect with its partners," senior author Ramon Sun, Ph.D., professor of biochemistry and molecular biology in the College of Medicine at University of Florida, told Fox News Digital. "The right amount is essential." What is glucosamine? "Glucosamine is a naturally occurring compound of sugar and an amino acid group that is a fundamental structural building block in the body," Neil Levin, senior nutrition education manager of Now, a manufacturer of glucosamine supplements in Illinois, told Fox News Digital. Glucosamine is concentrated in cartilage, the connective tissue that cushions joints, and is a component of larger molecules that help give cartilage its strength, elasticity and ability to retain water, he added. "Support for aging joints is the primary reason people take glucosamine as a dietary supplement," Levin said. ALZHEIMER'S BLOOD TESTS MAY PREDICT SYMPTOMS YEARS IN ADVANCE, BUT EXPERTS URGE CAUTION The body uses an internal "checkpoint" that naturally regulates how many of these sugar chains it produces, according to Sun. Supplemental glucosamine bypasses that "front gate" entirely — like a delivery truck pulling straight up to the loading dock, instantly boosting the supply of raw material used to make the sugar chains, the expert added. In the study, researchers analyzed thousands of patients with dementia, including Alzheimer's disease, as well as those with mild cognitive impairment, and then narrowed the group to those who were taking glucosamine. For those with mild cognitive impairment, taking the supplement didn't change their risk of death, but it did make them 25% more likely to progress to dementia. However, among individuals who already had dementia, glucosamine users had a higher mortality compared to similar non-users. POPULAR DRUGS FOR BONE HEALTH LINKED TO SIGNIFICANTLY LOWER ALZHEIMER'S RISK The researchers also examined brain tissue to understand what might be driving the association. "We found an excess of sugar chains on proteins in the Alzheimer’s brain," Sun said. Many of those proteins help nerve cells communicate, but the excess sugar chains may interfere with how they function, Sun said. He compared the effect to coating a key in too much wax — it is still the same key, but no longer fits the lock properly. "A brain affected by dementia and a healthy brain are different biological environments, and we shouldn't assume a supplement behaves the same way in both." Glucosamine is one of the materials cells use to make these sugar chains, according to Sun. Researchers also tracked how glucosamine was processed in mice, comparing its effects on healthy brains with those affected by Alzheimer’s-like disease. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "In our experiments, normal mice given glucosamine showed no increase in these sugar chains and no change in a memory test," Sun said. "But in mice with Alzheimer's-like disease, where the production line was already running too hot, glucosamine increased the sugar chains further and worsened performance on a memory test." Study limitations The researchers relied on medical records, which may not capture every supplement a patient was taking. "Health records tell us what was documented, not everything a person took," Sun said. "Over-the-counter supplements are not always recorded, and records don't reliably capture dose, brand or how consistently someone took it." An observational study looking at past records can find a signal, but can't prove one. Glucosamine users may also differ in factors such as arthritis, pain, mobility, frailty and medication use, Levin noted. The records also did not establish the exact supplement, dose, duration or consistency of use. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "The finding should therefore be treated as a safety signal that warrants controlled human research, but it did not — could not — reach a conclusion that glucosamine causes Alzheimer’s disease," Levin said. The next step is a well-designed, double-blind clinical trial to evaluate the impact of glucosamine on cognitive decline in patients with dementia. "For now, the evidence isn't strong enough to recommend any supplement for slowing [Alzheimer’s] disease, which is why doing this research properly, including the clinical trial we've called for, matters," Sun said. The study did not examine cognitively healthy people and does not suggest that glucosamine poses a risk to those who take it for joint health. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "A brain affected by dementia and a healthy brain are different biological environments, and we shouldn't assume a supplement behaves the same way in both," Sun said. He emphasized the importance of consulting with a doctor before starting or stopping a supplement. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "If you or a family member has a diagnosis of cognitive impairment or dementia and takes glucosamine, it's reasonable to bring it up at the next visit, as part of an ordinary conversation about what's in the medicine cabinet," the doctor advised. articles.title: Windows malware uses Grok AI to help stay hidden, researchers say
articles.summary: x47.c Windows malware uses xAI's Grok to maintain persistence on infected PCs while stealing passwords, browser cookies and API keys from victims.
articles.body: A new piece of Windows malware is giving cybercriminals a lot of ways to cause trouble from one infected PC. It can steal passwords, grab browser cookies, route internet traffic through your computer and even burn through paid AI credits. Then there is the part that caught my attention. The malware, called x47.c, can reportedly use xAI's Grok to help decide how to keep itself running on an infected Windows computer. Security researchers at Qrator Research Labs uncovered x47.c while tracking cybercrime activity. A threat actor using the name WraithTools has been advertising access to the malware, which comes with tools for stealing credentials and launching attacks. Qrator based its findings on the seller's advertisement, technical documentation, screenshots and follow-up messages, so the research shows what x47.c is advertised and designed to do rather than how widely it is currently infecting Windows PCs. Here's how it works, what the AI connection really means and the steps you can take to protect your Windows PC and accounts. AI IS NOW POWERING CYBERATTACKS, MICROSOFT WARNS Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways AI can help you get better health care. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class Get Better Healthcare with AI has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you prepare for appointments, remember important details, understand complicated medical information, research prescription questions and organize your next steps. No technical experience is needed. Plus, recordings of all our past classes are available, including How to Stop Spam, Phone Security and Financial Protection, each with a free downloadable checklist. Watch the free replays and get your checklists at CyberGuyLive.com How this Windows malware works Once x47.c infects a Windows computer, the attacker can remotely control it through a management panel. Think of that infected PC as one computer in a larger network of machines controlled by the same criminal. Security researchers call that a botnet, but the important part for you is much simpler: someone else can potentially use your computer without your permission. The operator can tell infected machines to launch online attacks. They can also steal information from those computers or use the victim's internet connection to route other traffic. Qrator found 18 advertised attack methods built into x47.c. Some can overwhelm websites and online services with traffic. Another targets something far newer: paid AI accounts. Hackers can burn through paid AI credits Many developers and businesses pay OpenAI, xAI and other AI companies based on how much they use their services. Access to those services often relies on a secret API key. You can think of that key as a password that lets an app communicate with an AI service and charge usage to an account. If an attacker gets a valid API key, x47.c includes a feature that can repeatedly send requests to the AI provider. Those requests can use up prepaid credits or increase the victim's bill. Qrator describes this as a "Denial of Wallet" attack. The victim's website could keep working normally while the AI account behind part of it quietly chews through its available balance. There is an important limit here. The attacker already needs a valid API key. x47.c does not magically break into an OpenAI or xAI account and create one. Still, that can become expensive quickly if an account allows automatic top-ups or high spending limits. Grok can help the malware stay on your PC The Grok connection sounds complicated, but the basic idea is pretty straightforward. Malware often tries to make sure it starts again after you reboot your computer. Security researchers call that persistence. x47.c includes what its seller calls an "AI Stealth" feature. According to Qrator, it can use Grok to look at the state of the infected computer and select from a predefined list of ways to maintain that access. Those options include adding programs that run when Windows starts and creating scheduled tasks that can launch automatically. Grok does not appear to freely invent new attacks or control everything the malware does. Instead, it helps choose among options that the malware already has. The malware can also fall back on its own built-in methods if the AI request fails. So, cutting off its access to Grok would not necessarily remove the infection. We reached out to xAI for comment on the reported use of Grok and the safeguards it has in place to detect this kind of activity but did not hear back before our deadline. Your saved passwords and browser sessions are targets For most Windows users, this may be the most important part. x47.c advertises the ability to steal passwords saved in your browser. It can also collect browser cookies, Discord tokens, cryptocurrency wallet information and tokens tied to AI websites. Browser cookies deserve special attention because some of them keep you signed in to websites. If malware steals an active login session, an attacker may be able to access an account without typing your password again. In some cases, changing the password alone may not immediately end a stolen session. That is why anyone dealing with an infected PC should also review active sessions and sign out of devices they do not recognize. AI MALWARE CAN REWRITE ITSELF TO EVADE DETECTION Your computer can also become someone else's internet connection x47.c includes another feature called a SOCKS5 proxy. In plain English, that means a criminal can potentially route internet traffic through the infected computer. Online activity generated by the attacker could then appear to come from the victim's internet connection. The malware's control panel lets operators see which infected computers are available to relay that traffic and whether those connections are still working. Meanwhile, the attacker can continue using the same infected machine to steal information or take part in online attacks. 9 ways to protect your Windows PC and accounts You do not need to understand every technical feature inside x47.c to protect yourself. These steps can reduce your chances of getting infected and limit the damage if malware does reach your computer. 1) Keep Windows updated Install Windows security updates promptly. Updates fix security weaknesses that attackers can use against PCs, even though Qrator has not identified a specific Windows vulnerability or infection method tied to x47.c. Go to Settings > Windows Update > Check for updates and install anything available. Also remember that legitimate Windows updates come through Windows itself. A website that suddenly tells you to download a Windows update should make you suspicious. CyberGuy has previously covered fake Windows update pages that actually install malware. 2) Use strong security software Keep strong antivirus or security software running and updated. Security tools can help catch malicious downloads and suspicious behavior before malware becomes deeply established on your computer. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. 3) Be careful about what you download Avoid software from unfamiliar download sites, unexpected email links or pop-ups telling you that something needs an urgent update. Also be especially cautious if a webpage tells you to open Windows Run, PowerShell or Command Prompt and paste something into it. Cybercriminals increasingly use that trick to persuade people to install malware themselves. We recently covered thousands of hacked websites using fake verification prompts to push malicious Windows commands. 4) Use unique passwords If malware steals one password, password reuse can turn one compromised account into several. Use a strong, unique password for every important account. A password manager can help create and store them. 5) Turn on two-factor authentication Enable two-factor authentication (2FA) wherever possible. It gives attackers another obstacle if they obtain your password. However, remember that malware capable of stealing active browser sessions creates another risk, so 2FA should be one layer of your protection rather than your only one. HALLUSQUATTING AI ATTACK COULD HIJACK YOUR COMPUTER 6) Sign out of active sessions after an infection If you believe your PC has been infected, changing passwords should not be your only account step. From a separate trusted device, review active login sessions for your email, financial accounts, social accounts and other important services. Sign out of unfamiliar sessions or use the service's option to sign out everywhere. Also revoke authentication tokens or connected apps you no longer recognize. Qrator specifically warns that removing the malware does not undo credentials or tokens that attackers may have already stolen. 7) Protect your AI API keys This one mainly applies to developers, businesses and anyone paying for AI through an API. Treat an API key like a password. Never publish it in a public code repository or leave it sitting in a document that other people can access. Review AI account usage and billing for requests you do not recognize. If you think a key has leaked, revoke it and create a new one. Also use spending limits, billing alerts and controls on automatic top-ups when your AI provider offers them. Those safeguards can limit how much an attacker could spend with a stolen key. 8) Disconnect the PC if you think it has been hacked If your computer suddenly behaves strangely or you discover malware, disconnect it from the internet. Then open your trusted security software directly and run a full scan. Do not call phone numbers in pop-ups or follow instructions from unexpected warnings on your screen. Our CyberGuy guide on what to do if your computer has been hacked walks through the next steps. 9) Change sensitive passwords from another trusted device If malware may have stolen information from your browser, use another clean device to change the passwords for your most important accounts. Start with your primary email account because password-reset messages for other services often go there. Then move to financial accounts and other sensitive services. After changing each password, review account activity and recovery information for anything you do not recognize. Kurt's key takeaways What gets my attention here isn't simply that the malware has the word AI attached to it. We've seen plenty of cyberthreats use AI as part of the sales pitch. What feels different with x47.c is how many jobs the attacker can handle from the same infected Windows PC. The malware can steal passwords and browser sessions, turn the computer into a traffic relay and help launch attacks. Then Grok can assist with choosing how the malware tries to keep its foothold on that machine. Still, the most useful lesson for you comes back to the security basics. Keep Windows updated, protect your accounts and be careful about what gets installed on your PC. And if you ever discover an infection, remember that cleaning the computer is only part of the job. You also have to assume passwords, browser sessions or other account access may already be in someone else's hands. Should AI companies be responsible for detecting when their tools are being used in malware and alerting authorities about that kind of activity? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com. articles.title: Woman, 42, Who Survived Colon Cancer 3 Times Shares Big Symptom She Hid At First
articles.summary: Woman survived colon cancer three times after being diagnosed in her teens, 20s and 30s. She shares her symptoms and how Lynch syndrome raises her cancer risk.
articles.body: At 42, Danielle Ripley-Burgess has survived colon cancer three times. She was first diagnosed at 17, then at 25 and then again at 39, making her a part of the trend of colorectal cancer rates surging in younger people. The Kansas City, Missouri, mom shared her story with TODAY.com and urged others to speak up about their symptoms. I had a cancer everyone thought old people get. Towards the end of my 8th grade year, when I was 14, I started seeing specks of blood in my stool when I’d go to the bathroom. I didn’t know what was happening. I downplayed it and tried to convince myself it was no big deal. I thought, I’m eating something red and that’s probably what I see. So I put myself on a “no red foods diet” and stopped eating anything that was red in color: everything from candy to pizza to salsa to raspberry Popsicles. It took me a while to accept that I was actually seeing blood, but I still hid it from just about everybody I knew. I was already embarrassed about puberty changes happening, so that on top of this thing was just too much. I didn’t want to be sick and I didn’t feel sick at first. But it was nagging at me, so about a year or two later, I did mention something to my mom. We looked it up online, and we saw it was probably hemorrhoids. She said blood in stool could also indicate something more serious, but it was something for people who were my grandparents’ ages. I was like, “great, I have hemorrhoids,” and went on with my life. In high school, seeing blood in the stool became something very normal, even as it got redder, darker and scarier. Eventually, I had some intense stomach pain, and I was getting fatigued. I couldn’t play volleyball anymore. I just wanted to come home and sleep. When I was 16, I told my boyfriend I thought I needed to see a doctor, but I didn’t tell him the details. My mom overheard one of our conversations and realized I was still seeing blood. She told my dad and they called the doctor, who sent me to a gastroenterologist right away. Just a few weeks after I turned 17, I was diagnosed with Stage 3 colon cancer. I had chemotherapy, radiation and surgery to remove the tumor. I also had surgery to move my ovaries up into my stomach to protect them from radiation. Doctors wanted to save the ovaries to preserve hormone function, but by elevating them, I couldn’t naturally conceive anymore. I thought I had beaten cancer. I was getting colonoscopies every three years, and after one of them, I woke up and saw the very same look on the doctor’s face that I had seen eight years prior. He saw a polyp that later turned out to be cancerous. I had no symptoms. At 25, I had Stage 1 colon cancer. Mentally and emotionally, it was way harder this time. I got really angry at a lot of things, but deep down just angry at God — how could you let this happen to me again? By this point, I was married, I had a house, I was working on a career, we’d been talking about adopting a child. All of a sudden, I realized I could lose all of these things. I don’t have any family history, and there was no explanation at first, but I found out I have Lynch syndrome, a genetic disease that puts you at a higher risk for several cancers, with colon and rectal cancers at the top of that list. I’m the first in my family to have the mutation. Knowing that the next target for Lynch syndrome was going to be either uterine cancer or ovarian cancer, I had a hysterectomy to prevent that. Part of my cancer story is a story of infertility. Adopting our daughter became our route to start a family. She’s 16 now, and we’ve also adopted a son, who is 5. I also underwent a subtotal colectomy, which took out all of my colon except about 13 inches. If you don’t have a colon anymore, your risk goes down. But in 2023, during my surveillance — which included yearly colonoscopies — my doctor found polyps and said, “It looks like cancer might be trying to come back again.” I decided to get a permanent ileostomy, where that remaining little bit of colon was removed. They sent it to pathology and found Stage 1 colon cancer — fortunately, all contained in that tissue. I wasn’t expecting it, but I also wasn’t completely shocked. Living with Lynch syndrome, I’m always aware that it’s a possibility. It’s always in my mind: Could this symptom or this pain or this odd thing happening in my body be something major? At this point, I’ve had just about every surgery I could have to prevent cancer. I have no colon left. I can never get colorectal cancer again, and that was a relief. More and more young people like me are getting colorectal cancer. If I could go back and tell my younger self something, it would be: Don’t be embarrassed about your body. If you’re seeing something with your body that’s uncomfortable and weird, and you’re not ready yet to tell a doctor, tell somebody — a friend or family member. Don’t sit in that place of: something is wrong with your body, and you don’t know what it is. Don’t sit there alone. Don’t downplay what you’re seeing. This interview was condensed and edited for clarity.

articles.title: What to know about pneumonic plague after woman in Russia dies from mysterious illness
articles.summary: The death of a 28-year-old woman who worked in an anti-plague laboratory in Russia is raising concerns about what caused her illness.
articles.body: The death of a 28-year-old woman who worked in an anti-plague laboratory in Russia is raising concerns about what caused her illness. The woman died Friday, according to the World Health Organization, with no cause of death confirmed. A Russian official said the woman died of pneumonia of “undetermined” origin and did not link her death to her work at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East. The U.S. State Department said, however, that it’s monitoring reports of a fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague in the Irkutsk region, in southeastern Siberia, in coordination with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. “While the circumstances of this reported case remain unconfirmed, plague is a serious bacterial disease that is treatable with antibiotics, particularly when recognized and treated early,” a spokeswoman for the Department of Health and Human Services said in a statement. “At this time, there is no indication from available reporting of a broader threat to the United States.” Key details aren’t known, including whether the woman was infected with plague at all and, if so, whether it was naturally occurring plague or bacteria studied in the lab. Scientists also don’t know how quickly her illness progressed and what treatment she received. Nearly 200 people who came into contact with the woman are under precautionary medical observation, according to Russian media. “Maybe it’s going to come out that she died from something unrelated and it was just a coincidence” that she worked in an anti-plague lab, said Lisa Morici, a microbiologist and immunologist in the Tulane University School of Medicine. Dr. Ashish Jha, the White House’s former Covid response coordinator, told NBC News in an interview, “If there were weapons programs, biological weapons programs in these labs, that would be much more concerning to me.” “We need to understand that now,” he added. The situation is still rapidly unfolding. But here’s what we know about the pneumonic plague, how it spreads and how dangerous it is. What is plague? Plague is an infection caused by Yersinia pestis bacteria. Known as the “Black Death” during the 14th century, the plague triggered several global pandemics over centuries before the discovery of antibiotics. It presents in three main forms: bubonic, pneumonic and septicemic, according to the World Health Organization. All three are caused by Yersinia pestis, but they occur in different parts of the body. Bubonic is the most common form, Morici said. It is primarily transmitted through bites of infected fleas or direct contact with infected rodents, which can cause painful, swollen lumps in the lymph nodes. It is usually not contagious. Left untreated, however, it can spread to the lungs and become pneumonic plague, which can pass from person to person through respiratory droplets, Morici said. Septicemic plague occurs when the bacteria grow and spread in the blood. How does pneumonic plague spread? Pneumonic plague can spread through the air when an infected person or animal coughs or sneezes. The respiratory droplets don’t travel very far, maybe three to six feet, said Dr. Dave Wagner, director of the Pathogen and Microbiome Institute at Northern Arizona University. “They drop to the ground pretty quickly.” It’s the rarest form of the disease, according to WHO. Dr. William Schaffer, an infectious diseases expert at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, said close contacts are most at risk. Pneumonic plague isn’t something that spreads “distantly across a room, but to face-to-face contacts,” he said. “It’s highly unlikely for most people to get the pneumonic form of the disease,” Morici said. Covid, for example, spreads like wildfire through the air, traveling beyond six feet. “It’s nothing like the Covid-19 pandemic,” she said. How deadly is it? While pneumonic plague is the rarest form of the disease, it’s also the deadliest. “It’s the one that’s so frightening because it can kill so quickly,” Morici said. It progresses remarkably fast, Wagner said. Symptoms typically appear within one to two days of exposure, and patients require treatment within 48 hours of showing symptoms to prevent fatal complications. Symptoms can include shortness of breath and coughing or blood in the phlegm. Because of how rapidly it attacks the respiratory system, public health experts consider this strain the most likely candidate for a biological attack, according to Morici. People with pneumonic plague are often quarantined, she said. Healthcare workers will often wear personal protective equipment, such as an N95 mask, or even a full body suit in case of accidental exposure. “We’re using the strictest levels of biocontainment,” she said. How is it treated? Antibiotics are highly effective against plague, including pneumonic plague. “This is why we don’t have big plague outbreaks anymore,” Wagner said. Schaffner said there’s no evidence to suggest that the plague bacteria are evolving in a way to become resistant to antibiotics. “We will not turn 2026 into the Middle Ages, where the Black Death caused vast amounts of death throughout Europe. That will not happen.” Wagner said he has no reason to believe this suspected case of plague is “going to take off and spread.” “The plague that we have today is the same plague that was the scourge of humanity for so long during great pandemics,” he said. Is the plague found in the U.S.? About seven cases of plague are reported in the U.S. each year, according to the CDC. Most occur in rural parts of the Southwest, including Arizona, California, Colorado and New Mexico. These are areas where Yersinia pestis bacteria naturally circulate among wild rodents like prairie dogs and their fleas. Most people are treated quickly with antibiotics and recover. Deaths from the plague in the U.S. are rare but do happen. Last July, a man in Arizona died of pneumonic plague after he was exposed to sick cats. Within a week, the man went to an emergency department with shallow breathing, a fast heart rate, chest pain and a dry cough. Despite getting antibiotics and oxygen, the man died within eight hours of his admission to the hospital. Testing later showed he had pneumonic plague.

articles.title: Niamh O'Brien: Dancer and wife of Michael Flatley dies, aged 52
articles.summary: She was a renowned Irish dancer who performed the lead role of Saoirse in the Lord of the Dance.
articles.body:
Niamh O'Brien, a former lead performer in Lord of the Dance and the wife of Riverdance star Michael Flatley, has died at the age of 52.

Announcing her death on social media on Monday, Flatley said his "heart is broken".

"My gorgeous bride of twenty years has gone to the Lord in Heaven."

O'Brien was a renowned Irish dancer who performed the lead role of Saoirse in the Lord of the Dance shows.

Flatley described her as "the most loving mother, wife and person and our lives will never be the same without her".

The couple had a son, Michael St James, who was born in 2007.

A representative for Flatley said that O'Brien died peacefully at the Beacon Hospital in Dublin after an illness, Irish national broadcaster RTÉ reports.

"The Flatley and O'Brien families are devastated by Niamh's sudden passing and have asked that their privacy be respected as they come to terms with this heartbreaking loss," said the representative.

"They express their sincere gratitude to the doctors, nurses and staff at Beacon Hospital who cared for Niamh over the past few weeks, and to everyone who has offered their kindness and support to the family."

images.caption: O'Brien was a renowned Irish dancer and married Flatley in 2006

articles.title: Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak is the country’s largest in three decades
articles.summary: Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak is now the largest in the U.S. in three decades.
articles.body: Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak is now the largest in the U.S. in three decades. On Monday, the state surpassed South Carolina’s outbreak from earlier this year, which topped out at 997. That outbreak was contained within six months. Pennsylvania’s outbreak, which began in late April, shows no sign of slowing. “I would bet that this goes on for at least another three to six months,” said Dr. John Goldman, an infectious disease expert at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center. “We have seen an increase in vaccinations, but we aren’t seeing enough people get vaccinated to stop the epidemic.” On Monday, the Pennsylvania Department of Health reported 1,004 measles cases, with 198 hospitalizations. Nearly a third of the cases have been in children. Among the pediatric measles cases, 18% have needed hospitalization. Dehydration has become a common problem, particularly among babies and younger children, said Dr. Evan Shirey, a pediatric infectious disease physician at Penn State Health Golisano Children’s Hospital in Hershey. Doctors are also seeing young patients with liver problems. “One of the more common things that the measles virus can do is cause hepatitis or infection of the liver,” Shirey said. “These children will feel very sick, very nauseous, with abdominal pain and vomiting, and they can’t take a bottle or can’t keep food or liquid down.” Other children are developing severe and irreversible neurological damage because of brain inflammation, or encephalitis, Shirey said. “In some of these cases, it’s a child who can’t recognize their own mother, who’s disoriented and confused,” Shirey said. Still others have developed secondary bacterial infections. Five people in the state have died, according to the health department. Those people include a teenager with severe brain inflammation and a 40-year-old woman with a history of asthma, as well as two babies. One of those babies was a newborn who died after his mother went into labor a month early. There are few details about the fifth person who died, other than the person hadn’t been vaccinated and lived in Lancaster County, where the bulk of measles cases are. Lancaster County is home to the nation’s largest Amish population, with approximately 44,000 residents as of 2025. There is nothing in the religion that is inherently anti-vaccine, but historically, their vaccination rates have been lower than those of the general population, Goldman said. According to an NBC News investigation, 88.5% of kindergartners in 2024 had the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine. A vaccination rate of at least 95% is the accepted level of herd immunity needed to protect against a measles outbreak. “There’s nothing special about Lancaster. The exact same thing could happen in any county in the country that has a large percentage of unvaccinated people,” Goldman said. “If it hasn’t happened yet, it’s only because measles hasn’t gotten into that county yet.” The outbreak in South Carolina, which ended in April, was previously the largest in approximately 30 years, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. That outbreak was linked to a community of people who emigrated from Ukraine over the past few decades. State health officials credited a massive surge in vaccinations with bringing its outbreak to a halt. In the northwestern corner of the state, where the outbreak was centered, nearly 15,000 MMR vaccinations were given during the South Carolina outbreak, up 82% compared with the previous year, according to the South Carolina Department of Public Health. As of Monday, the Pennsylvania health department said it’s given just 8,843 MMR doses so far in response to the outbreak. Ohio is also dealing with a growing measles outbreak along the border it shares with Pennsylvania. As of Thursday, Ohio had logged 210 measles cases, with 13 hospitalizations. Most cases are concentrated in the northeastern part of the state, in Geauga, Ashtabula and Wayne counties.

articles.title: Thrombectomy: 'My treatment was a miracle' says stroke patient
articles.summary: An expanded service means the time of day or night a stroke occurs is no longer a barrier to treatment.
articles.body:
When Gemma O'Hara woke up in the night with "intense pain" in her neck, sickness and vertigo she knew something was "not right".

The 40-year-old, who had just come back from holiday, had suffered a brain stem stroke.

Gemma was able to have a thrombectomy, which removes blood clots and restores blood flow to the brain, a procedure she has said is a "miracle treatment" that has enabled her to recover well.

Northern Ireland's regional thrombectomy service, which had only been available between 08:00 and 17:00 is now operating 24 hours a day, seven days a week after a £5m investment through Stormont's Programme for Government (PfG) Elective Care funding.

Gemma, from Ballymena in County Antrim, said the expansion is "amazing" because of the difference the treatment made to her recovery.

"You have to get treated so fast. You can't let time go past when it's to do with your brain," she said. "If I didn't get it in time I wouldn't be the way I am now."

'I may not be here if my stroke was at different time'

New stroke suite brings life-saving treatment to Kent

'I had a stroke at the weekend so didn't get a thrombectomy'

The mother-of three had the stroke in September 2025 and said that, while her symptoms were not classic stroke symptoms, she knew she needed medical help.

By the time she arrived at the Antrim Area Hospital, she had numbness, could not walk or talk and felt "locked in my body".

She was scanned and given thrombolysis - clot-busting medication - before being transferred to the Royal Victoria Hospital in Belfast for a thrombectomy.

Gemma said that within minutes of having her procedure she was "sitting up, back to myself again" and waiting for her family to arrive.

"It's a miracle treatment because I was so unwell and for something that can happen fairly quickly like that, and to recover so well, it's amazing," she said.

'I was going to the gym and trying to look after myself'

She said having a stroke was "so unexpected".

"I was always working, going to the gym and trying to look after myself.

"So for everybody that was a big shock for me to have a stroke because they always thought I would have been the fittest one."

Gemma said one of her "biggest fears" had been the possibly of having another stroke during the night, when thrombectomy was previously unavailable.

She said the 24/7 service gives her "peace of mind" that she would be able to receive treatment if it happened again.

The expanded service, which began on 14 September, means the time of day or night a stroke occurs is no longer a barrier to accessing treatment.

Dr Patricia Gordon, stroke consultant at Belfast Health Trust, said about 10% of patients who have a stroke have a large clot that can be removed through a thrombectomy.

She said the procedure increases a patient's chances of making a good recovery by more than 50% and reduces the risk of death by almost 20%.

"Whenever you have a stroke that requires a thrombectomy - that was one of the major and main arteries being blocked in the brain.

"Those are the most severe type of strokes that you have.

"Untreated, there's a risk of death from those types of strokes."

She said that if patients survive they can be left with "significant disability" depending on where the blockage is - but "it could be weakness down one side, loss of speech or sometimes loss of function altogether then as well".

The consultant said the impact of having a thrombectomy is "quite significant".

"You're going from a very dependent state to a nearly independent state again by more than 50% if you can get the clot out in good time," she said.

The service will build capacity towards 300 thrombectomy procedures annually, about double what it has been doing during reduced hours.

Gordon said the stroke team has advocated to expand this service for some time and it is "transformational" for people.

She said having it 24/7 means that it is available to all patients and there will be staff there to perform it.

"You can see that there's a huge amount of staff that are needed to be able to fill rotas and to be there to be able to treat patients," she said.

"It will largely transform patients' lives from being potentially significantly dependent to independent."

The service is delivered at the Royal Victoria Hospital Belfast through a regional pathway involving stroke teams at the Causeway, Antrim Area, Royal Victoria, Ulster, Craigavon Area, Daisy Hill, Altnagelvin and South West Acute hospitals.

Artificial Intelligence-supported imaging is being used to help clinicians rapidly identify patients who may benefit.

In June 2022, a commitment to expand the regional thrombectomy service to 24/7 provision was published in the Reshaping Stroke Care Action Plan.

According to the Department of Health, about 3,000 people have a stroke each year in Northern Ireland, which is one person every three hours, and more than 43,000 stroke survivors live in the community.

In 2024, Nisra recorded 883 stroke deaths.

Health Minister Robbie Butler said Northern Ireland was the first of the UK nations to provide a 24/7 thrombectomy service for its entire population, which he described as a "landmark moment".

"Thrombectomy is one of the most significant advances in modern stroke medicine and can dramatically improve a patient's chances of recovery," he said.

articles.title: New York state declares measles disaster amid resurgence of disease in US
articles.summary: The US had largely eliminated measles by 2000 but has seen several outbreaks amid declining vaccination rates.
articles.body:
New York state has declared a disaster emergency over an outbreak of measles, as cases of the disease that had once been all but eliminated in the United States continue to rise .

New York Governor Kathy Hochul said on Monday that she was temporarily expanding the ability of health professionals to administer measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccines.

“No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease,” Hochul said in a statement, adding that New York has recorded 108 cases of measles this year, as of October 3. The declaration will remain in effect through November 4.

Hochul’s announcement marks the first such declaration since measles cases began to tick up in 2025. She said that seven cases were recorded in New York City and 101 elsewhere in the state.

Hochul’s declaration says 92 cases have been recorded since July 15 in a handful of rural communities with insufficient vaccination rates.

Officials in neighbouring Pennsylvania also announced that the state has surpassed 1,000 measles cases this year, the largest outbreak in the US in the last three decades. Outbreaks have also been recorded in Texas, Utah, Ohio and South Carolina.

Health experts attribute the resurgence to a decline in vaccination rates below the 95 percent rate they say is necessary to prevent outbreaks.

Critics say the decline has been spurred by an anti-vaccination movement that has surged in popularity and gained advocates inside the administration of President Donald Trump , including Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr.

The US had eliminated the domestic spread of measles by 2000, with the last outbreak of more than 1,000 cases occurring over several years in New York City in the early 1990s.

International officials from the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) are set to meet in November to determine whether the US and Mexico will retain their measles-free status, or whether the public health designations will be updated.

“PAHO reiterates the importance of maintaining high and homogeneous vaccination coverage, strengthening epidemiological surveillance, and ensuring timely outbreak response, as essential pillars to halt transmission and sustain measles elimination in the countries of the Americas,” the organisation said in a previous statement.

articles.title: Widowed twice: A Gaza mother’s story of loss and survival
articles.summary: A young mother has lost two husbands and two children during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
articles.body:
Gaza City, Gaza — For three years, Nisreen Touman has gone to bed every night in tears, remembering all she has lost since the start of Israel’s war on Gaza in October 2023.

By the time Nisreen was 34, she had been widowed twice. First, she lost her husband and her two children in June 2024. Then in July 2025, eight months after she remarried, Nisreen lost her second husband while she was pregnant.

Before Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, Nisreen lived a happy and stable life in her home in Nuseirat, central Gaza, with her husband, Sami, 35, and their two children, Mahmoud and Laith, who were aged five and two at the time of their deaths.

“I had a home and a complete family. I got along with my husband, and we were friends,” she says, fighting back her tears.

On June 8, 2024, Nisreen was returning home with her husband and children after visiting extended family, who had been displaced to al-Mawasi in Khan Younis.

“We arrived and the children were playing in the street. Everything was normal. I was upstairs with my husband when suddenly we started hearing heavy, very close, bombing and gunfire.”

Her husband rushed outside to bring their children and his brother’s and sister’s children inside, where 25 members of her family were staying.

He then went outside again to see what was happening, as aircraft flew overhead.

“That was the last time I saw him. I later learned that he had been killed by a gunshot to the head from a quadcopter that was flying over the area that day,” she said.

Minutes later, while trying to calm the children as the bombing and gunfire continued, the house was targeted by an Israeli aircraft.

“I lost consciousness for a few moments, then woke up to thick dust that completely blocked my view,” she said.

“As the dust began to clear, I started to understand our place was bombed. I heard the family screaming and saw blood and body parts. I started shouting, ‘My children, my children.’”

Nisreen breaks down as she recalls seeing her two children lying on the ground. One had suffered severe head injuries, while the other appeared to be sleeping.

“I knew from that moment that I had lost them. It was clear that they were dead,” she says, recalling how she was unable to move from the shock.

Her husband’s brother came and placed the children in her arms.

“I could not speak. I was completely unable to speak, just tears running silently,” she said. “Everyone around me was screaming and crying.”

For two hours, Nisreen held her children in her arms as the family, including those who were injured, remained trapped in the damaged home as gunfire and bombing continued.

After repeated requests to the International Committee of the Red Cross for help, the family were eventually evacuated to a hospital.

The killing of Nisreen’s family came on one of the bloodiest days of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. On June 8, 2024, Israeli forces launched a military operation in the Nuseirat refugee camp, central Gaza, to rescue four Israeli captives who had been held following the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on October 7, 2023.

The United Nations said 89 inhabited houses and residential buildings were targeted in nearly four hours of bombing. Gaza’s Health Ministry said that 274 Palestinians were killed and 698 wounded on that day alone.

Eighteen members of Nisreen’s husband’s family were killed, including her husband and children, her sister Sabreen, 36, her mother-in-law, two of her husband’s brothers and their children, as well as members of the extended family.

Nisreen returned alone to her family’s tent in al-Mawasi south of Gaza, where she struggled with the trauma and grief of losing her family. Four and a half months later, Nisreen found herself facing a difficult decision when her late sister’s husband, who was also her first husband’s brother, proposed to her.

He wanted to marry Nisreen and have her help take care of their four children, who had lost their mother.

“I strongly opposed it at first. I did not want to start a family or get married,” Nisreen said. She eventually agreed because she wanted to care for her departed sister’s children, especially the youngest, who was only one year old.

Nisreen does not hide the fact that there were no romantic feelings behind her second marriage. “I had lost my husband, and he had lost his wife. I had lost my children, and the four children had lost their mother,” she said.

The marriage allowed two people to fill the roles of the ones they lost. Nisreen found in her sister’s children a small comfort for the absence of her own.

But her new life came with significant challenges, especially during the first months. She was still grieving her first husband and her children, as she and her new husband attempted to adjust to each other.

Their different personalities and the new situation presented challenges, but gradually their lives became more stable. Nisreen even considered having another child.

“I used to see my children who had died, in my dreams every day. I would drift into thoughts about them, and they never left my mind,” she said. “So, with encouragement from my mother, I decided to become pregnant and experience motherhood again.”

But eight months later, on July 8, 2025, Nisreen faced something she had never imagined: the loss of her second husband.

“Mohammed woke up, had breakfast with the children and said he was going to see a friend. A few moments later, we heard a huge explosion,” she said.

Shortly after, Nisreen was told by a neighbour that Mohammed had been killed in a strike on a group of people near al-Awda Hospital in Nuseirat.

For Nisreen, this second loss was even harder to bear than the first. After believing she had finally settled into a new sense of stability, her life was once again turned upside down.

“I felt like I was back at zero again,” she said. “I thought about the baby who had not yet been born, the children of my sister who had now lost both their mother and father, and the new loss I was living through.”

The remaining months of her pregnancy were heavy for Nisreen. Four months after Mohammed’s death, she gave birth to their daughter, Sidra.

Sidra’s birth brought back to Nisreen the pain of everything she had lost – her two children, her first husband and Mohammed.

While her daughter, who turns one in October, has brought Nisreen a “little compensation” for three years of sadness, it pains her that she will grow up without a father.

“Becoming a mother again brought me joy, but that feeling was deeply incomplete. She was a little compensation,” she said

Caring for Sidra has become Nisreen’s main priority.

“I have become more isolated. I prefer to stay quiet for hours and focus on my daughter,” Nisreen says. “I am afraid of making any new choices or trying to start another life after everything that happened to me.”

Nisreen now lives with Sidra at her family’s home in Gaza, while her late sister’s four children are being cared for by their grandfather. She visits them from time to time.

No matter how much time passes, she says she is unable to overcome the series of tragedies that have shaped her life.

“I never imagined I would go through all of this in my life. Sometimes it feels like I’m in an Indian film because of everything that has happened,” she said. “But under the war, unfortunately, anything is possible.”
